scenes.tts: When you turn your own head, why does the reflex that steadies your head not fight you?
scenes.visual: Title card: Pass On the Surprise. A person turning their head; a reflex arrow pushes back, marked with a question mark.
scenes.narration: When you turn your own head, why does the reflex that steadies your head not fight you?

scenes.tts: That reflex treats head motion as a disturbance. Your own turn would look like one.
scenes.visual: The reflex arrow opposes the turn. Caption: a disturbance?
scenes.narration: That reflex treats head motion as a disturbance. Your own turn would look like one.

scenes.tts: Does the ear tell the two apart? In alert monkeys, canal afferents responded to both.
scenes.visual: Schematic afferent responses with similar rate modulation for a self-made turn and a matched imposed turn; individual spike times differ. Label: schematic; similar sensitivity, not identical spike trains; Cullen and Minor, 2002.
scenes.narration: Does the ear tell the two apart? In alert monkeys, canal afferents responded to both.

scenes.tts: So any cancelling must happen in the brain.
scenes.visual: An arrow from the ear into the brainstem; label: cancel here.
scenes.narration: So any cancelling must happen in the brain.

scenes.tts: Roy and Cullen recorded vestibular-only neurons, thought to drive the neck reflex that steadies the head.
scenes.visual: A brainstem neuron lights for head motion and stays dark for an eye movement; it connects to neck muscles. Label: Roy and Cullen, 2004.
scenes.narration: Roy and Cullen recorded vestibular-only neurons, thought to drive the neck reflex that steadies the head.

scenes.tts: The brain has two clues to a self-made turn. One is the motor command, which predicts the neck's feedback. The other is the neck's actual sense of stretch.
scenes.visual: Two inputs arrive: a motor-command arrow labelled prediction, and a neck-feedback arrow labelled actual.
scenes.narration: The brain has two clues to a self-made turn. One is the motor command, which predicts the neck's feedback. The other is the neck's actual sense of stretch.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. A passive turn. An active turn with matching neck feedback. An active turn with mismatched feedback. Which ones drive the neuron strongly?
scenes.visual: Three columns: passive; active, matched; active, mismatched. Bars hidden. Question: which respond strongly?
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. A passive turn. An active turn with matching neck feedback. An active turn with mismatched feedback. Which ones drive the neuron strongly?

scenes.visual: the question stays on screen

scenes.tts: The passive turn did. So did the active turn with mismatched feedback. Only the matched active turn was cancelled.
scenes.visual: Bars reveal, made-up numbers: 40, 4, and climbing back toward 40 spikes per second.
scenes.narration: The passive turn did. So did the active turn with mismatched feedback. Only the matched active turn was cancelled.

scenes.tts: In this made-up example, nearly all of the response is cancelled.
scenes.visual: On screen: sensitivity 2.0 falls to 0.2; 90 percent cancelled. Label: made-up numbers.
scenes.narration: In this made-up example, nearly all of the response is cancelled.

scenes.tts: This is not the ear switching off. The afferents kept firing.
scenes.visual: The afferent trace keeps firing beneath the cancelled central response.
scenes.narration: This is not the ear switching off. The afferents kept firing.

scenes.tts: This muting may help keep the head-steadying reflex from opposing a turn you intend. It does not mean you stop sensing your own head movements.
scenes.visual: Caption: a possible help to the head reflex; you still feel the turn.
scenes.narration: This muting may help keep the head-steadying reflex from opposing a turn you intend. It does not mean you stop sensing your own head movements.

scenes.tts: A prediction must stay right. Brooks and colleagues recorded neurons in a cerebellar output nucleus, the rostral fastigial nucleus. Their monkeys turned their heads against a resistive load.
scenes.visual: Label: Brooks, Carriot and Cullen, 2015; rostral fastigial neurons. A head turning against a resisting dial.
scenes.narration: A prediction must stay right. Brooks and colleagues recorded neurons in a cerebellar output nucleus, the rostral fastigial nucleus. Their monkeys turned their heads against a resistive load.

scenes.tts: As the animals adapted, these neurons' vestibular sensitivity fell. When the load was suddenly removed, it rose again.
scenes.visual: A sensitivity curve falls over trials, then spikes upward on a catch trial marked load removed.
scenes.narration: As the animals adapted, these neurons' vestibular sensitivity fell. When the load was suddenly removed, it rose again.

scenes.tts: These are recordings. They show what the neurons did, not that they caused the learning.
scenes.visual: Caption: recordings, correlational.
scenes.narration: These are recordings. They show what the neurons did, not that they caused the learning.

scenes.tts: Finally, a vestibular implant stimulates the canal branches of the nerve when both ears have lost their signal.
scenes.visual: An implant with three electrodes reaching the three canal branches.
scenes.narration: Finally, a vestibular implant stimulates the canal branches of the nerve when both ears have lost their signal.

scenes.tts: It varies its pulses to represent head rotation. It does not recreate the nerve's two natural channels, and it sends no otolith signal.
scenes.visual: Pulse train whose rate follows head rotation. Caption: rotation only; not the natural two-channel code; no otolith signal.
scenes.narration: It varies its pulses to represent head rotation. It does not recreate the nerve's two natural channels, and it sends no otolith signal.

scenes.tts: In eight adults, some balance measures improved. Hearing in the implanted ear fell in all but one.
scenes.visual: Two panels: posture and gait, some improved; hearing in the implanted ear, reduced in all but one, severely in three. Label: Chow and colleagues, 2021.
scenes.narration: In eight adults, some balance measures improved. Hearing in the implanted ear fell in all but one.

scenes.tts: A cohort this small shows feasibility and a trade-off, not that the device works for everyone.
scenes.visual: Caption: feasibility and a trade-off.
scenes.narration: A cohort this small shows feasibility and a trade-off, not that the device works for everyone.

scenes.tts: The nerve reports motion on two channels. Where neck feedback matches the prediction, these head-posture neurons pass on mainly the surprise.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: report it twice, on two overlapping channels; pass on the surprise, in the tested head-posture neurons, with matched neck feedback.
scenes.narration: The nerve reports motion on two channels. Where neck feedback matches the prediction, these head-posture neurons pass on mainly the surprise.
